title: Fire, heat and carbon monoxide
summary: Which fire extinguisher fits which fire, how to use one, and when to leave instead. Also carbon monoxide rules for generators, stoves and heaters, safe heating, wood stove and chimney safety, and the energy in common fuels and firewood.

steps.text: In a fire, decide fight or leave first. If it is not small and contained, get out and call 9-1-1.
steps.warn: Never put water on grease, electrical or flammable-liquid fires.

steps.text: Match the extinguisher class to what is burning, then Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep.
Running anything that burns fuel during a power cut? Read the carbon monoxide section first and put alarms on every level.
steps.warn: Generators, grills, camp stoves and gas ovens never go indoors, not even in a garage.

steps.text: For wood heat: dry wood, yearly chimney sweep, ashes in a covered metal can outdoors. Use the fuel tables to plan how much to store.

notes:
## Fire triangle
A fire needs heat, fuel and oxygen. Remove one and it goes out. Extinguishers also break the chemical chain reaction (OSHA).
- **Cool it:** water, on ordinary materials only.
- **Smother it:** a lid on a pan, CO2, dry chemical.
- **Starve it:** remove or shut off the fuel.

## Which extinguisher
| Class | Burning | Use | Never use |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | Wood, paper, cloth, rubber, many plastics | Water, ABC dry chemical | |
| B | Gasoline, oil, paint, solvents, grease | CO2, BC or ABC dry chemical | Water |
| C | Live electrical equipment | CO2, dry chemical | Water |
| D | Magnesium, titanium, sodium, potassium | Special dry powder only | Water |
| K | Cooking oil and fat | Wet chemical | Water |

Canada and the US use the same letters (CCOHS, OSHA). Read the label: ABC covers A, B and C (Toronto). On a deep fat fryer, use neither water nor CO2 (OSHA). Inspect monthly, service yearly (CCOHS). Keep one in the kitchen (Ready.gov).

## Using one: PASS
1. **Pull** the pin.
2. **Aim** at the base of the fire from about 3 m (10 ft).
3. **Squeeze** the handle.
4. **Sweep** side to side until it looks out (Toronto).

Keep watching it and never turn your back (Toronto). Most extinguishers empty in 10 to 60 seconds (CCOHS).

## Fight or leave
Fight only if all of these are true (Toronto):
- The fire is small and not spreading.
- Everyone is leaving or out, and 9-1-1 has been called.
- You have a clear escape route.
- You know how to use this extinguisher.

Otherwise leave, shut the door, and call 9-1-1 from outside. Leave at once if you do not know what is burning or which extinguisher fits (CCOHS). A fire can become life-threatening in 2 minutes. In smoke, crawl low. If a door is hot, use another way out (Ready.gov).

## Common fires
| Fire | Do | Never |
|---|---|---|
| Grease in a pan | Turn off the burner. Slide a lid over the pan and leave it on until cool (Cambridge FD) | Pour water, or move the pan |
| Electrical | Cut power only if the plug or breaker is safe to reach. Class C extinguisher only (Manitoba Hydro) | Use water, or fight a large fire |
| Clothes | Stop, drop, roll. Cool the burn with cool water for at least 10 minutes (see First aid essentials) | |

## Carbon monoxide (CO)
CO builds up when fuel burns without enough air. It can harm you before you notice it (Health Canada).
- **Symptoms:** headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain, confusion, often mistaken for flu. Sleeping people can die without symptoms (CDC). Higher levels bring poor vision, then coma and death (Health Canada).
- **Never indoors, or in a garage, shed, tent or camper:** generators, charcoal or BBQ grills, camp stoves, flameless chemical heaters, or a gas oven for heat (CDC, Health Canada). Never idle a vehicle in an attached garage, even with the door open (CDC).
- **Appliances:** have furnaces, water heaters and fuel-burning heaters serviced yearly (CDC, Health Canada).
- **Generators:** at least 6 m (20 ft) from any building, exhaust aimed away from windows, doors and vents. A shut-off switch does not make indoor use safe (Health Canada, CPSC).
- **Alarms:** battery or battery-backup, on every level and outside sleeping areas. Test monthly (CPSC). Replace as the maker says, or every 5 years (CDC). Smoke alarms do not detect CO (Health Canada).
- **Alarm sounds or symptoms:** go outside now, do not hunt for the cause, call 9-1-1 from outside, return only when a professional clears it (Health Canada). No help coming: see [When no help is coming](#ref/reference_fire_heat/when_no_help_is_coming).

## Safe indoor heating
- Keep heaters 1 m (3 ft) from beds, curtains, furniture and papers (CPSC, Ready.gov).
- Never leave one on while you sleep, or unattended in a closed room. Refuel only when cool (CPSC).
- Plug electric heaters into a wall outlet, never a power strip or extension cord (CPSC, Manitoba Hydro).
- No kerosene, propane or oil heaters in closed spaces unless made for indoor use (Health Canada). Kerosene: K-1 fuel, no overfilling, ventilate (Ready.gov).

## Wood heat and chimney fires
- Have chimney and stove pipe inspected and cleaned yearly. Check monthly for damage or blockage (Ready.gov, CSIA).
- Creosote feeds chimney fires. Smouldering fires, unseasoned wood, closed dampers and overloaded stoves make it (CMHC, CSIA).
- Burn wood at 15 to 20% moisture. Fresh logs can be half water (CMHC).
- Keep furniture, firewood and anything that burns at least 1 m (3 ft) from the stove, and further if its label says so. Walls are another matter: an unlabelled stove needs 1,200 mm (48 in) from combustible walls (NRCan wood heating; see [installing a stove](#guides/build_stove_install)). Burn only wood, never plastics, rubber, garbage or coal (Georgian Bay).
- Ashes stay hot for days. Use a covered metal container, outdoors, 3 m (10 ft) from buildings (Georgian Bay, Ontario OFMEM).
- **Chimney fire signs:** loud cracking or popping, low rumble, dense smoke, hot smell, flames or smoke at the top. Masonry chimney fires reach about 1,100 °C (2,000 °F). **Get everyone out and call 9-1-1 at once** if it can be reached: don’t wait to judge whether the flue is damaged. No fire service: see [When no help is coming](#ref/reference_fire_heat/when_no_help_is_coming). Have a certified sweep inspect it before burning again (CSIA).

## Energy in fuels
| Fuel | MJ per kg | Btu per lb |
|---|---|---|
| Firewood, air-dry (about 25% moisture) | 14 to 15 | 6,200 to 6,500 |
| Wood pellets (10% moisture or less) | 18 to 20 | 7,700 to 8,500 |
| Wood chips (about 45% moisture) | 10 to 11 | 4,300 to 4,700 |
| Heating oil | 42 | 18,000 |
| Propane | 50 | 21,500 |
| Natural gas | 43 | 19,000 |

High heating values, so real stoves deliver less (NRCan, Missouri Conservation).

| Wood, per cord (3.6 m³, 128 ft³) | GJ | Million Btu |
|---|---|---|
| Hickory | 30.7 | 29.1 |
| Black locust | 29.6 | 28.1 |
| White oak | 28.5 | 27.0 |
| Red oak | 26.7 | 25.3 |
| Ash | 24.9 | 23.6 |
| Elm | 22.6 | 21.4 |
| Shortleaf pine | 20.0 | 19.0 |
| Cottonwood | 17.0 | 16.1 |

Dense woods hold more energy per cord. Value depends on density and dryness (Missouri Conservation). Hardwoods like oak and maple suit cold weather. Birch and poplar suit mild weather (CMHC).

## When no help is coming

**Chimney fire**
- Get everyone out first. A flue fire reaches about 1,100 °C (2,000 °F) and can crack the chimney out of sight (CSIA white paper).
- Close the stove's air inlets, doors and damper. This usually ends the flames but may leave creosote glowing (CSIA white paper, Livermore FD).
- Do not open the stove door or cleanout to look. Fresh air can make it flare (CSIA white paper, Fire Eng tips).
- No water into the stove or flue. It can crack the liner or cause a steam blast (Fire Eng guide, Livermore FD).
- Chimney extinguisher stick or flare: use as the maker says, then keep stove doors, glass doors and air inlets shut (Natural Handyman, FireRescue1).
- Only if you can do it with no risk to yourself, spray down the roof with a garden hose, not the chimney (Natural Handyman). Watch walls, ceiling and attic near the flue for heat or smoke (Fire Eng guide). Keep checking the chimney's surface in each room it passes through for at least 2 to 3 hours after the fire is out (Natural Handyman).
- Do not burn again until the flue is swept and checked for cracked tiles, failed mortar and warped pipe, by a qualified chimney sweep if you can reach one (CSIA after-fire).

**House fire**
- You may have as little as two minutes (NFPA). Crawl low. If a door is hot, use another way out. If trapped, seal door cracks with cloth and signal at a window (Ready.gov).
- Get out and stay out. Never go back for people, pets or things (NFPA).
- Flames from windows can ignite a house 1.8 m away in under 80 seconds (NIST). Warn neighbours at once.

**Carbon monoxide**
- Get into fresh air at once. Open a door on the way out or switch the appliance off only if that takes seconds. Do not go back in to do it, or to look for the cause (EPA, Health Canada). A rescuer can be overcome too. If breathing has stopped, give CPR (OSHA CO fact sheet).
- In fresh air the body clears half the CO every 4 to 6 hours (OSHA CO outline). Memory, mood and thinking problems can appear later (OSHA CO outline, CDC CO clinical).
- Do not run the appliance again until it is repaired and its flue checked (EPA).
